Because this establishes the pristine awareness of emptiness as the basis of characteristics and teaches that no relative phenomena whatsoever exist within it, this is the fourth statement that clearly teaches the great other-emptiness Madhyamaka. According to those renowned as proponents of self-emptiness, it is inappropriate to say 'in emptiness there is no form', because, since the basis of characteristics, emptiness, is unestablished, it is never reasonable to negate the characteristic of form separately within it; and if one negates form and so on when the emptiness of self-emptiness is already established to the mind, it absurdly follows that one is negating what has already been negated. According to them, the words of the sūtra would have to be altered and recited as 'the absence of form is emptiness'.

heading: ༡༣༽གནས་དང་གནས་མིན་ལ་མཁས་པར་བྱ་བ།
translation: there is also no non-attainment of the state of the result from what is not a cause. The meaning of the sūtra regarding all of these should be grasped as follows: For saṃsāric sentient beings and all meditators on the path, the dharmadhātu arises as the illusion of foundational phenomena such as form, and as various appearances of the phenomena of the path and the result, and they do not see it in the actual form of that abiding nature. Therefore, since all those appearances of the foundation and the path appear while being non-existent, having established them as such during the time of hearing and reflection, one should, through meditation, let all phenomena from the aggregate of form up to non-attainment dissolve naturally into the essence of awareness, and this demonstrates that one must rest in meditative equipoise within that pristine awareness of natural emptiness. This shares the same essential point as explaining the three absences of nature, because in the established meaning of the explanation by way of three, the ultimate expanse existing perfectly arises solely as being merely empty of adventitious conventionalities. Therefore, the thought of some who consider those two ways of explanation to be contradictory is a display of great arrogance due to not understanding. Thus, among the six, by training in the three—aggregates, elements, and sense sources—one becomes skilled in the defining characteristics of dharmatā; by training in dependent origination and the four truths, one becomes skilled in adopting, discarding, engaging, and turning back; and by training in the possible and the impossible, one becomes skilled in causes, conditions, and results.

there is also no non-attainment of the state of the result from what is not a cause. The meaning of the sūtra regarding all of these should be grasped as follows: For saṃsāric sentient beings and all meditators on the path, the dharmadhātu arises as the illusion of foundational phenomena such as form, and as various appearances of the phenomena of the path and the result, and they do not see it in the actual form of that abiding nature. Therefore, since all those appearances of the foundation and the path appear while being non-existent, having established them as such during the time of hearing and reflection, one should, through meditation, let all phenomena from the aggregate of form up to non-attainment dissolve naturally into the essence of awareness, and this demonstrates that one must rest in meditative equipoise within that pristine awareness of natural emptiness. This shares the same essential point as explaining the three absences of nature, because in the established meaning of the explanation by way of three, the ultimate expanse existing perfectly arises solely as being merely empty of adventitious conventionalities. Therefore, the thought of some who consider those two ways of explanation to be contradictory is a display of great arrogance due to not understanding. Thus, among the six, by training in the three—aggregates, elements, and sense sources—one becomes skilled in the defining characteristics of dharmatā; by training in dependent origination and the four truths, one becomes skilled in adopting, discarding, engaging, and turning back; and by training in the possible and the impossible, one becomes skilled in causes, conditions, and results.

heading: ༡༥༽ དེ་རྟོགས་པའི་ལམ་གྱི་ཕན་ཡོན།
translation: "Therefore, bodhisattvas" and so forth. The phrase "because there is no attainment" illuminates the end, and it clearly applies to everything extending back to "there is no form." Stating "attainment" primarily intends that all the others are also subsumed within the statement that, in the abiding nature, neither what is suitable nor what is unsuitable to be produced as a result by a producing cause is established. Therefore, just as nothing from form up to non-attainment is established in the abiding nature of things, practitioners of the Mahāyāna must meditate in that way; "therefore," in the very essence of the pristine awareness in meditative equipoise of the bodhisattvas, because things that are causes and results, along with actions and agents, are primordially unestablished,

[15-1] source:
​ལྔ་པ་བདེན་པ་ལ་མཁས་པར་བསླབ་པ་ནི།
[15-1] translation already produced for this document:

[15-2] source:
​སྟོང་ཉིད་ཀྱི་སྟེང་ན་ཕུང་ཁམས་སྐྱེ་མཆེད་རྟེན་འབྲེལ་མ་གྲུབ་པ་དེ་བཞིན་དུ། ​སྟོང་ཉིད་ཀྱི་ཡེ་ཤེས་ལ། ​སྡུག་བསྔལ་བདེན་པ་ཐམས་ཅད་དང་། ​ཀུན་འབྱུང་བདེན་པ་ཐམས་ཅད་དང་།​འགོགས་བདེན་གསར་ཐོབ་རྣམས་དང་། ​ལམ་བདེན་རྣམས་ངོ་བོས་མེད་དོ། །​དེ་ཡང་སྤང་བླང་གི་གཞི་འགོག་བདེན་ནི་སྟོང་ཉིད་ཡིན་ལ། ​བླང་དོར་བྱེད་པའི་བདེན་པ་བཞི་ཅར་འགོག་གོ །

Just as the aggregates, elements, sense sources, and dependent origination are unestablished within emptiness, similarly, in the pristine awareness of emptiness, all truths of suffering, all truths of origin, newly attained truths of cessation, and truths of the path are non-existent in essence. Furthermore, the truth of cessation, the basis for abandoning and adopting, is emptiness, and it negates all four truths that involve adopting and discarding.

དྲུག་པ་གནས་དང་གནས་མ་ཡིན་པ་ལ་མཁས་པར་བསླབ་པ་ནི།
[16-1] translation already produced for this document:

[16-2] source:
​སྟོང་པ་ཉིད་ཀྱི་ཡེ་ཤེས་ལ། ​ལམ་གྱིས་བསྡུས་པའི་ཡེ་ཤེས་མེད་ཅིང་། ​དེས་ངེས་པར་འབྱུང་བ་ཡང་མེད།
[16-2] translation already produced for this document:

There is also no attainment of the respective states of causes and effects of things, and

[16-4] source:
​རྒྱུ་མིན་ལས་འབྲས་བུའི་གནས་སྐབས་མ་ཐོབ་པ་ཡང་མེད་དོ། །​དེ་དག་ཐམས་ཅད་ཀྱི་དོན་གྱི་མདོ་འདི་ལྟར་གཟུང་སྟེ། ​འཁོར་བའི་སེམས་ཅན་རྣམས་དང་། ​ལམ་སྒོམ་པ་པོ་ཐམས་ཅད་ལ། ​ཆོས་དབྱིངས་དེ་གཟུགས་སོགས་གཞིའི་ཆོས་ཀྱི་འཁྲུལ་པ་དང་། ​ལམ་དང་འབྲས་བུའི་ཆོས་ཀྱི་སྣང་བ་སྣ་ཚོགས་སུ་ཤར་ཞིང་། ​གནས་ལུགས་དེའི་རང་གཟུགས་སུ་མ་མཐོང་ལ། ​དེས་ན་གཞི་ལམ་གྱི་སྣང་བ་དེ་དག་ཐམས་ཅད་མེད་བཞིན་དུ་སྣང་བ་ཡིན་པའི་ཕྱིར། ​ཐོས་བསམ་གྱི་དུས་སུ་དེ་ལྟར་གཏན་ལ་ཕབ་ནས། ​སྒོམ་པས་གཟུགས་ཕུང་ནས་མ་ཐོབ་པའི་བར་གྱི་ཆོས་ཐམས་ཅད་རིག་པའི་ངོ་བོར་རང་སང་དུ་བཏང་སྟེ། ​རང་བཞིན་སྟོང་ཉིད་ཀྱི་ཡེ་ཤེས་དེ་ལ་མཉམ་པར་འཇོག་དགོས་པར་བསྟན་ཏོ། །ངོ་བོ་ཉིད་མེད་གསུམ་དུ་འཆད་པ་དང་འདི་གནད་གཅིག་པས། ​གསུམ་དུ་བཤད་པའི་གྲུབ་དོན་ལའང་དོན་དམ་དབྱིངས་ཡང་དག་པར་གནས་པ་དེ། ​གློ་བུར་ཀུན་རྫོབ་ཀྱིས་སྟོངས་པ་ཙམ་ཁོ་ན་འབྱུང་བའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །​དེས་ན་ཁ་ཅིག་བཤད་ཚུལ་དེ་གཉིས་འགལ་བར་སེམས་པ་ནི། ​མ་གོ་བ་ཡུས་ཆེ་པའི་ཚུལ་ལོ། །​དེ་ལྟར་དྲུག་ལས་ཕུང་ཁམས་སྐྱེ་མཆེད་གསུམ་ལ་བསླབ་པས་ནི། ​ཆོས་ཉིད་ཀྱི་མཚན་ཉིད་ལ་མཁས་པར་འགྱུར་ལ། ​རྟེན་འབྲེལ་དང་བདེན་བཞི་ལ་བསླབ་པས་བླང་དོར་འཇུག་ལྡོག་ལ་མཁས་ཤིང་། ​གནས་དང་གནས་མ་ཡིན་པ་ལ་བསླབ་པས་རྒྱུ་རྐྱེན་འབྲས་བུ་ལ་མཁས་པར་འགྱུར་བ་ཡིན་ནོ། །
[16-4] translation already produced for this document:
there is also no non-attainment of the state of the result from what is not a cause. The meaning of the sūtra regarding all of these should be grasped as follows: For saṃsāric sentient beings and all meditators on the path, the dharmadhātu arises as the illusion of foundational phenomena such as form, and as various appearances of the phenomena of the path and the result, and they do not see it in the actual form of that abiding nature. Therefore, since all those appearances of the foundation and the path appear while being non-existent, having established them as such during the time of hearing and reflection, one should, through meditation, let all phenomena from the aggregate of form up to non-attainment dissolve naturally into the essence of awareness, and this demonstrates that one must rest in meditative equipoise within that pristine awareness of natural emptiness. This shares the same essential point as explaining the three absences of nature, because in the established meaning of the explanation by way of three, the ultimate expanse existing perfectly arises solely as being merely empty of adventitious conventionalities. Therefore, the thought of some who consider those two ways of explanation to be contradictory is a display of great arrogance due to not understanding. Thus, among the six, by training in the three—aggregates, elements, and sense sources—one becomes skilled in the defining characteristics of dharmatā; by training in dependent origination and the four truths, one becomes skilled in adopting, discarding, engaging, and turning back; and by training in the possible and the impossible, one becomes skilled in causes, conditions, and results.

​རྒྱུ་མིན་ལས་འབྲས་བུའི་གནས་སྐབས་མ་ཐོབ་པ་ཡང་མེད་དོ། །​དེ་དག་ཐམས་ཅད་ཀྱི་དོན་གྱི་མདོ་འདི་ལྟར་གཟུང་སྟེ། ​འཁོར་བའི་སེམས་ཅན་རྣམས་དང་། ​ལམ་སྒོམ་པ་པོ་ཐམས་ཅད་ལ། ​ཆོས་དབྱིངས་དེ་གཟུགས་སོགས་གཞིའི་ཆོས་ཀྱི་འཁྲུལ་པ་དང་། ​ལམ་དང་འབྲས་བུའི་ཆོས་ཀྱི་སྣང་བ་སྣ་ཚོགས་སུ་ཤར་ཞིང་། ​གནས་ལུགས་དེའི་རང་གཟུགས་སུ་མ་མཐོང་ལ། ​དེས་ན་གཞི་ལམ་གྱི་སྣང་བ་དེ་དག་ཐམས་ཅད་མེད་བཞིན་དུ་སྣང་བ་ཡིན་པའི་ཕྱིར། ​ཐོས་བསམ་གྱི་དུས་སུ་དེ་ལྟར་གཏན་ལ་ཕབ་ནས། ​སྒོམ་པས་གཟུགས་ཕུང་ནས་མ་ཐོབ་པའི་བར་གྱི་ཆོས་ཐམས་ཅད་རིག་པའི་ངོ་བོར་རང་སང་དུ་བཏང་སྟེ། ​རང་བཞིན་སྟོང་ཉིད་ཀྱི་ཡེ་ཤེས་དེ་ལ་མཉམ་པར་འཇོག་དགོས་པར་བསྟན་ཏོ། །ངོ་བོ་ཉིད་མེད་གསུམ་དུ་འཆད་པ་དང་འདི་གནད་གཅིག་པས། ​གསུམ་དུ་བཤད་པའི་གྲུབ་དོན་ལའང་དོན་དམ་དབྱིངས་ཡང་དག་པར་གནས་པ་དེ། ​གློ་བུར་ཀུན་རྫོབ་ཀྱིས་སྟོངས་པ་ཙམ་ཁོ་ན་འབྱུང་བའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །​དེས་ན་ཁ་ཅིག་བཤད་ཚུལ་དེ་གཉིས་འགལ་བར་སེམས་པ་ནི། ​མ་གོ་བ་ཡུས་ཆེ་པའི་ཚུལ་ལོ། །​དེ་ལྟར་དྲུག་ལས་ཕུང་ཁམས་སྐྱེ་མཆེད་གསུམ་ལ་བསླབ་པས་ནི། ​ཆོས་ཉིད་ཀྱི་མཚན་ཉིད་ལ་མཁས་པར་འགྱུར་ལ། ​རྟེན་འབྲེལ་དང་བདེན་བཞི་ལ་བསླབ་པས་བླང་དོར་འཇུག་ལྡོག་ལ་མཁས་ཤིང་། ​གནས་དང་གནས་མ་ཡིན་པ་ལ་བསླབ་པས་རྒྱུ་རྐྱེན་འབྲས་བུ་ལ་མཁས་པར་འགྱུར་བ་ཡིན་ནོ། །

there is also no non-attainment of the state of the result from what is not a cause. The meaning of the sūtra regarding all of these should be grasped as follows: For saṃsāric sentient beings and all meditators on the path, the dharmadhātu arises as the illusion of foundational phenomena such as form, and as various appearances of the phenomena of the path and the result, and they do not see it in the actual form of that abiding nature. Therefore, since all those appearances of the foundation and the path appear while being non-existent, having established them as such during the time of hearing and reflection, one should, through meditation, let all phenomena from the aggregate of form up to non-attainment dissolve naturally into the essence of awareness, and this demonstrates that one must rest in meditative equipoise within that pristine awareness of natural emptiness. This shares the same essential point as explaining the three absences of nature, because in the established meaning of the explanation by way of three, the ultimate expanse existing perfectly arises solely as being merely empty of adventitious conventionalities. Therefore, the thought of some who consider those two ways of explanation to be contradictory is a display of great arrogance due to not understanding. Thus, among the six, by training in the three—aggregates, elements, and sense sources—one becomes skilled in the defining characteristics of dharmatā; by training in dependent origination and the four truths, one becomes skilled in adopting, discarding, engaging, and turning back; and by training in the possible and the impossible, one becomes skilled in causes, conditions, and results.

Stating "attainment" primarily intends that all the others are also subsumed within the statement that, in the abiding nature, neither what is suitable nor what is unsuitable to be produced as a result by a producing cause is established. Therefore, just as nothing from form up to non-attainment is established in the abiding nature of things, practitioners of the Mahāyāna must meditate in that way; "therefore," in the very essence of the pristine awareness in meditative equipoise of the bodhisattvas, because things that are causes and results, along with actions and agents, are primordially unestablished,

​རྒྱུ་མིན་ལས་འབྲས་བུའི་གནས་སྐབས་མ་ཐོབ་པ་ཡང་མེད་དོ། །​དེ་དག་ཐམས་ཅད་ཀྱི་དོན་གྱི་མདོ་འདི་ལྟར་གཟུང་སྟེ། ​འཁོར་བའི་སེམས་ཅན་རྣམས་དང་། ​ལམ་སྒོམ་པ་པོ་ཐམས་ཅད་ལ། ​ཆོས་དབྱིངས་དེ་གཟུགས་སོགས་གཞིའི་ཆོས་ཀྱི་འཁྲུལ་པ་དང་། ​ལམ་དང་འབྲས་བུའི་ཆོས་ཀྱི་སྣང་བ་སྣ་ཚོགས་སུ་ཤར་ཞིང་། ​གནས་ལུགས་དེའི་རང་གཟུགས་སུ་མ་མཐོང་ལ། ​དེས་ན་གཞི་ལམ་གྱི་སྣང་བ་དེ་དག་ཐམས་ཅད་མེད་བཞིན་དུ་སྣང་བ་ཡིན་པའི་ཕྱིར། ​ཐོས་བསམ་གྱི་དུས་སུ་དེ་ལྟར་གཏན་ལ་ཕབ་ནས། ​སྒོམ་པས་གཟུགས་ཕུང་ནས་མ་ཐོབ་པའི་བར་གྱི་ཆོས་ཐམས་ཅད་རིག་པའི་ངོ་བོར་རང་སང་དུ་བཏང་སྟེ། ​རང་བཞིན་སྟོང་ཉིད་ཀྱི་ཡེ་ཤེས་དེ་ལ་མཉམ་པར་འཇོག་དགོས་པར་བསྟན་ཏོ། །ངོ་བོ་ཉིད་མེད་གསུམ་དུ་འཆད་པ་དང་འདི་གནད་གཅིག་པས། ​གསུམ་དུ་བཤད་པའི་གྲུབ་དོན་ལའང་དོན་དམ་དབྱིངས་ཡང་དག་པར་གནས་པ་དེ། ​གློ་བུར་ཀུན་རྫོབ་ཀྱིས་སྟོངས་པ་ཙམ་ཁོ་ན་འབྱུང་བའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །​དེས་ན་ཁ་ཅིག་བཤད་ཚུལ་དེ་གཉིས་འགལ་བར་སེམས་པ་ནི། ​མ་གོ་བ་ཡུས་ཆེ་པའི་ཚུལ་ལོ། །​དེ་ལྟར་དྲུག་ལས་ཕུང་ཁམས་སྐྱེ་མཆེད་གསུམ་ལ་བསླབ་པས་ནི། ​ཆོས་ཉིད་ཀྱི་མཚན་ཉིད་ལ་མཁས་པར་འགྱུར་ལ། ​རྟེན་འབྲེལ་དང་བདེན་བཞི་ལ་བསླབ་པས་བླང་དོར་འཇུག་ལྡོག་ལ་མཁས་ཤིང་། ​གནས་དང་གནས་མ་ཡིན་པ་ལ་བསླབ་པས་རྒྱུ་རྐྱེན་འབྲས་བུ་ལ་མཁས་པར་འགྱུར་བ་ཡིན་ནོ། །

there is also no non-attainment of the state of the result from what is not a cause. The meaning of the sūtra regarding all of these should be grasped as follows: For saṃsāric sentient beings and all meditators on the path, the dharmadhātu arises as the illusion of foundational phenomena such as form, and as various appearances of the phenomena of the path and the result, and they do not see it in the actual form of that abiding nature. Therefore, since all those appearances of the foundation and the path appear while being non-existent, having established them as such during the time of hearing and reflection, one should, through meditation, let all phenomena from the aggregate of form up to non-attainment dissolve naturally into the essence of awareness, and this demonstrates that one must rest in meditative equipoise within that pristine awareness of natural emptiness. This shares the same essential point as explaining the three absences of nature, because in the established meaning of the explanation by way of three, the ultimate expanse existing perfectly arises solely as being merely empty of adventitious conventionalities. Therefore, the thought of some who consider those two ways of explanation to be contradictory is a display of great arrogance due to not understanding. Thus, among the six, by training in the three—aggregates, elements, and sense sources—one becomes skilled in the defining characteristics of dharmatā; by training in dependent origination and the four truths, one becomes skilled in adopting, discarding, engaging, and turning back; and by training in the possible and the impossible, one becomes skilled in causes, conditions, and results.

"Therefore, bodhisattvas" and so forth. The phrase "because there is no attainment" illuminates the end, and it clearly applies to everything extending back to "there is no form." Stating "attainment" primarily intends that all the others are also subsumed within the statement that, in the abiding nature, neither what is suitable nor what is unsuitable to be produced as a result by a producing cause is established. Therefore, just as nothing from form up to non-attainment is established in the abiding nature of things, practitioners of the Mahāyāna must meditate in that way; "therefore," in the very essence of the pristine awareness in meditative equipoise of the bodhisattvas, because things that are causes and results, along with actions and agents, are primordially unestablished,

heading: ༡༦༽ ལམ་དེས་རྟོགས་པའི་འབྲས་བུ་བཤད་པ།
translation: having meditated with the six ways of being skilled, have awakened and will awaken to unsurpassed, perfect awakening. In the explicit teaching of all of those, solely the selflessness of phenomena is stated; the selflessness of persons is intended to arise by implication of that. However, the statement that seems to say the bodhisattva does not meditate on the selflessness of persons means that having asserted the aggregates, the basis of negation, to exist, they do not engage in such a manner of meditating on the selflessness of persons that meditates on the absence of 'I' and 'self' upon them; rather, the selflessness of persons that has the aspect of freedom from conceptual elaboration is indeed an object to be meditated upon by the sons of the victorious ones. Since the non-establishment of any 'I' or 'self' in the abiding nature is the selflessness of persons, and whatever objects of knowledge of appearance and sound have never existed in the abiding nature is the selflessness of phenomena, because the former is subsumed within the latter, by meditating on the selflessness of phenomena, meditating on the selflessness of persons is implicitly established.

​རྒྱུ་མིན་ལས་འབྲས་བུའི་གནས་སྐབས་མ་ཐོབ་པ་ཡང་མེད་དོ། །​དེ་དག་ཐམས་ཅད་ཀྱི་དོན་གྱི་མདོ་འདི་ལྟར་གཟུང་སྟེ། ​འཁོར་བའི་སེམས་ཅན་རྣམས་དང་། ​ལམ་སྒོམ་པ་པོ་ཐམས་ཅད་ལ། ​ཆོས་དབྱིངས་དེ་གཟུགས་སོགས་གཞིའི་ཆོས་ཀྱི་འཁྲུལ་པ་དང་། ​ལམ་དང་འབྲས་བུའི་ཆོས་ཀྱི་སྣང་བ་སྣ་ཚོགས་སུ་ཤར་ཞིང་། ​གནས་ལུགས་དེའི་རང་གཟུགས་སུ་མ་མཐོང་ལ། ​དེས་ན་གཞི་ལམ་གྱི་སྣང་བ་དེ་དག་ཐམས་ཅད་མེད་བཞིན་དུ་སྣང་བ་ཡིན་པའི་ཕྱིར། ​ཐོས་བསམ་གྱི་དུས་སུ་དེ་ལྟར་གཏན་ལ་ཕབ་ནས། ​སྒོམ་པས་གཟུགས་ཕུང་ནས་མ་ཐོབ་པའི་བར་གྱི་ཆོས་ཐམས་ཅད་རིག་པའི་ངོ་བོར་རང་སང་དུ་བཏང་སྟེ། ​རང་བཞིན་སྟོང་ཉིད་ཀྱི་ཡེ་ཤེས་དེ་ལ་མཉམ་པར་འཇོག་དགོས་པར་བསྟན་ཏོ། །ངོ་བོ་ཉིད་མེད་གསུམ་དུ་འཆད་པ་དང་འདི་གནད་གཅིག་པས། ​གསུམ་དུ་བཤད་པའི་གྲུབ་དོན་ལའང་དོན་དམ་དབྱིངས་ཡང་དག་པར་གནས་པ་དེ། ​གློ་བུར་ཀུན་རྫོབ་ཀྱིས་སྟོངས་པ་ཙམ་ཁོ་ན་འབྱུང་བའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །​དེས་ན་ཁ་ཅིག་བཤད་ཚུལ་དེ་གཉིས་འགལ་བར་སེམས་པ་ནི། ​མ་གོ་བ་ཡུས་ཆེ་པའི་ཚུལ་ལོ། །​དེ་ལྟར་དྲུག་ལས་ཕུང་ཁམས་སྐྱེ་མཆེད་གསུམ་ལ་བསླབ་པས་ནི། ​ཆོས་ཉིད་ཀྱི་མཚན་ཉིད་ལ་མཁས་པར་འགྱུར་ལ། ​རྟེན་འབྲེལ་དང་བདེན་བཞི་ལ་བསླབ་པས་བླང་དོར་འཇུག་ལྡོག་ལ་མཁས་ཤིང་། ​གནས་དང་གནས་མ་ཡིན་པ་ལ་བསླབ་པས་རྒྱུ་རྐྱེན་འབྲས་བུ་ལ་མཁས་པར་འགྱུར་བ་ཡིན་ནོ། །

there is also no non-attainment of the state of the result from what is not a cause. The meaning of the sūtra regarding all of these should be grasped as follows: For saṃsāric sentient beings and all meditators on the path, the dharmadhātu arises as the illusion of foundational phenomena such as form, and as various appearances of the phenomena of the path and the result, and they do not see it in the actual form of that abiding nature. Therefore, since all those appearances of the foundation and the path appear while being non-existent, having established them as such during the time of hearing and reflection, one should, through meditation, let all phenomena from the aggregate of form up to non-attainment dissolve naturally into the essence of awareness, and this demonstrates that one must rest in meditative equipoise within that pristine awareness of natural emptiness. This shares the same essential point as explaining the three absences of nature, because in the established meaning of the explanation by way of three, the ultimate expanse existing perfectly arises solely as being merely empty of adventitious conventionalities. Therefore, the thought of some who consider those two ways of explanation to be contradictory is a display of great arrogance due to not understanding. Thus, among the six, by training in the three—aggregates, elements, and sense sources—one becomes skilled in the defining characteristics of dharmatā; by training in dependent origination and the four truths, one becomes skilled in adopting, discarding, engaging, and turning back; and by training in the possible and the impossible, one becomes skilled in causes, conditions, and results.

[18-3] source:
​མཁས་པའི་ཚུལ་དྲུག་གིས་བསྒོམས་པས་བླ་ན་མེད་པ་ཡང་དག་པར་རྫོགས་པའི་བྱང་ཆུབ་ཏུ་སངས་རྒྱས་ཟིན་པ་དང་། ​སངས་རྒྱས་བར་འགྱུར་རོ། །​དེ་དག་ཐམས་ཅད་ཀྱི་དངོས་བསྟན་ལ་ཆོས་ཀྱི་བདག་མེད་ཁོ་ན་གསུངས་ཏེ། ​གང་ཟག་གི་བདག་མེད་ནི་དེའི་ཤུགས་ལ་འབྱུང་པར་དགོངས་སོ། །​འོན་ཀྱང་གང་ཟག་གི་བདག་མེད་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔས་མི་སྒོམ་པ་ལྟར་གསུངས་པ་ནི། ​དགག་གཞི་ཕུང་པོ་ཡོད་པར་བྱས་ནས། ​དེའི་སྟེང་དུ་ང་བདག་མེད་པར་སྒོམ་པའི་གང་ཟག་གི་བདག་མེད་སྒོམ་ཚུལ་དེ་འདྲ་མི་བྱེད་ཅེས་པའི་དོན་ཡིན་གྱི། ​སྤྲོས་བྲལ་གྱི་རྣམ་པ་ཅན་གྱི་གང་ཟག་གི་བདག་མེད་ནི་རྒྱལ་སྲས་རྣམས་ཀྱིས་བསྒོམ་བྱ་ཁོ་ནའོ། །​གནས་ཚུལ་ལ་ང་བདག་གང་ཡང་མ་གྲུབ་པ་ནི། ​གང་ཟག་གི་བདག་མེད་ཡིན་ལ། ​གནས་ཚུལ་ལ་སྣང་གྲགས་ཀྱི་ཤེས་བྱ་གང་ཡང་ཡོད་མ་མྱོང་བ་ནི་ཆོས་ཀྱི་བདག་མེད་ཡིན་པས། ​སྔ་མ་ཕྱི་མའི་ནང་དུ་འདུས་པའི་ཕྱིར། ​ཆོས་ཀྱི་བདག་མེད་བསྒོམས་པས་གང་ཟག་གི་བདག་མེད་སྒོམ་པར་ཤུགས་ལ་འགྲུབ་པོ། །​

having meditated with the six ways of being skilled, have awakened and will awaken to unsurpassed, perfect awakening. In the explicit teaching of all of those, solely the selflessness of phenomena is stated; the selflessness of persons is intended to arise by implication of that. However, the statement that seems to say the bodhisattva does not meditate on the selflessness of persons means that having asserted the aggregates, the basis of negation, to exist, they do not engage in such a manner of meditating on the selflessness of persons that meditates on the absence of 'I' and 'self' upon them; rather, the selflessness of persons that has the aspect of freedom from conceptual elaboration is indeed an object to be meditated upon by the sons of the victorious ones. having meditated with the six ways of being skilled, have awakened and will awaken to unsurpassed, perfect awakening. In the explicit teaching of all of those, solely the selflessness of phenomena is stated; the selflessness of persons is intended to arise by implication of that. However, the statement that seems to say the bodhisattva does not meditate on the selflessness of persons means that having asserted the aggregates, the basis of negation, to exist, they do not engage in such a manner of meditating on the selflessness of persons that meditates on the absence of 'I' and 'self' upon them; rather, the selflessness of persons that has the aspect of freedom from conceptual elaboration is indeed an object to be meditated upon by the sons of the victorious ones. Since the non-establishment of any 'I' or 'self' in the abiding nature is the selflessness of persons, and whatever objects of knowledge of appearance and sound have never existed in the abiding nature is the selflessness of phenomena, because the former is subsumed within the latter, by meditating on the selflessness of phenomena, meditating on the selflessness of persons is implicitly established.

[18-3] source:
​མཁས་པའི་ཚུལ་དྲུག་གིས་བསྒོམས་པས་བླ་ན་མེད་པ་ཡང་དག་པར་རྫོགས་པའི་བྱང་ཆུབ་ཏུ་སངས་རྒྱས་ཟིན་པ་དང་། ​སངས་རྒྱས་བར་འགྱུར་རོ། །​དེ་དག་ཐམས་ཅད་ཀྱི་དངོས་བསྟན་ལ་ཆོས་ཀྱི་བདག་མེད་ཁོ་ན་གསུངས་ཏེ། ​གང་ཟག་གི་བདག་མེད་ནི་དེའི་ཤུགས་ལ་འབྱུང་པར་དགོངས་སོ། །​འོན་ཀྱང་གང་ཟག་གི་བདག་མེད་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔས་མི་སྒོམ་པ་ལྟར་གསུངས་པ་ནི། ​དགག་གཞི་ཕུང་པོ་ཡོད་པར་བྱས་ནས། ​དེའི་སྟེང་དུ་ང་བདག་མེད་པར་སྒོམ་པའི་གང་ཟག་གི་བདག་མེད་སྒོམ་ཚུལ་དེ་འདྲ་མི་བྱེད་ཅེས་པའི་དོན་ཡིན་གྱི། ​སྤྲོས་བྲལ་གྱི་རྣམ་པ་ཅན་གྱི་གང་ཟག་གི་བདག་མེད་ནི་རྒྱལ་སྲས་རྣམས་ཀྱིས་བསྒོམ་བྱ་ཁོ་ནའོ། །​གནས་ཚུལ་ལ་ང་བདག་གང་ཡང་མ་གྲུབ་པ་ནི། ​གང་ཟག་གི་བདག་མེད་ཡིན་ལ། ​གནས་ཚུལ་ལ་སྣང་གྲགས་ཀྱི་ཤེས་བྱ་གང་ཡང་ཡོད་མ་མྱོང་བ་ནི་ཆོས་ཀྱི་བདག་མེད་ཡིན་པས། ​སྔ་མ་ཕྱི་མའི་ནང་དུ་འདུས་པའི་ཕྱིར། ​ཆོས་ཀྱི་བདག་མེད་བསྒོམས་པས་གང་ཟག་གི་བདག་མེད་སྒོམ་པར་ཤུགས་ལ་འགྲུབ་པོ། །​
[18-3] translation already produced for this document:
having meditated with the six ways of being skilled, have awakened and will awaken to unsurpassed, perfect awakening. In the explicit teaching of all of those, solely the selflessness of phenomena is stated; the selflessness of persons is intended to arise by implication of that. However, the statement that seems to say the bodhisattva does not meditate on the selflessness of persons means that having asserted the aggregates, the basis of negation, to exist, they do not engage in such a manner of meditating on the selflessness of persons that meditates on the absence of 'I' and 'self' upon them; rather, the selflessness of persons that has the aspect of freedom from conceptual elaboration is indeed an object to be meditated upon by the sons of the victorious ones. Since the non-establishment of any 'I' or 'self' in the abiding nature is the selflessness of persons, and whatever objects of knowledge of appearance and sound have never existed in the abiding nature is the selflessness of phenomena, because the former is subsumed within the latter, by meditating on the selflessness of phenomena, meditating on the selflessness of persons is implicitly established.

heading: ༡༧༽ ཕན་ཡོན་དང་བཅས་པའི་གཟུངས་སྔགས་བསྟན་པ།
translation: Because the dharmakāya is undeceptive, it is "not false," and because its own essence is unchanging and permanent, it is truly established; and because this mantra is also of the same essence as that dharmakāya, it is undeceptive and not false, and thus it "should be known as the truth." That is the meaning, and this is the fifth statement clearly demonstrating the great Madhyamaka of other-emptiness. The actual mantra of prajñāpāramitā is that which abides in the mind-stream of a Buddha, so it is the actual dharmakāya and is actually truly established; and that which appears to the speech and mind of trainees and ordinary beings, although not actual in that way, is the cause for attaining that, so it is indeed a truth that does not deceive in the attainment of the result. However, it is taught that mantras such as this spoken by the victorious ones belong to the consummate nature and are undefiled, even down to when they arise in the minds of ordinary beings who have not entered the path.

translation: "tadyathā" means "it is thus." "gate" is gone and realized. Appearing twice means realizing the relative and realizing the ultimate. "para" is supreme, which is the abiding nature. "gate" is realized. Again, "para" is supreme; "sam" is perfect; "gate" is realized. "bodhi" is awakening, which is the pristine awareness that unmistakably realizes the abiding nature of the two truths. It means awakening, becoming of one taste with the dharmadhātu. "svāhā" means "establish the foundation," which accomplishes the end of the mantra.

That is the meaning, and this is the fifth statement clearly demonstrating the great Madhyamaka of other-emptiness. The actual mantra of prajñāpāramitā is that which abides in the mind-stream of a Buddha, so it is the actual dharmakāya and is actually truly established; and that which appears to the speech and mind of trainees and ordinary beings, although not actual in that way, is the cause for attaining that, so it is indeed a truth that does not deceive in the attainment of the result. heading: ༢༠༽རྩ་བའི་གསུམ་པ། ​ཡི་རང་མངོན་པར་བསྟོད་པ།
translation: Here, if the Tathāgata had not spoken his concordant approval in that way, the retinues would not have gained belief and thus would not have been joyful and satisfied. Furthermore, in accordance with the perceptions of other disciples, Śāriputra would have been discouraged and doubtful, thinking, "Was my question inappropriate?"; and Avalokiteśvara too would have been discouraged and doubtful, thinking, "Is it possible that I did not explain the answer well?" However, since the Teacher spoke the concordant approval, "Excellent," Śāriputra was joyful that his own question was good; the noble Avalokiteśvara too was supremely joyful, knowing that his answer to the question turned out well; and the other retinues also gained delight and satisfaction, since they gained belief and their doubts were severed. Moreover, if some were to say here, "If this profound sūtra belongs to the sūtras of the middle turning, it is inappropriate for it to teach the Madhyamaka of other-emptiness," and, "If it teaches that, there would be no difference in profundity between the middle and final [turnings]," they should be answered as follows: The intention of all three turnings is also the Madhyamaka of other-emptiness, and even in the first and middle turnings there are some words that clearly teach it explicitly. In the turning that ascertains the ultimate, it is taught more clearly and extensively, without being hidden but made manifest or expounded boundlessly, than in both the [first] turning and the middle one. Thus, there is a difference of superior and inferior among the three turnings, and since their intention is also the same, those two faults do not apply. Therefore, regarding the explicit teaching of this sūtra, it clearly teaches the common other-emptiness, while it explains the uncommon meaning of the heart of the Sugata, which is permanent, steadfast, eternal, and possessing all aspects, by way of hidden meaning.

Here, if the Tathāgata had not spoken his concordant approval in that way, the retinues would not have gained belief and thus would not have been joyful and satisfied. Furthermore, in accordance with the perceptions of other disciples, Śāriputra would have been discouraged and doubtful, thinking, "Was my question inappropriate?"; and Avalokiteśvara too would have been discouraged and doubtful, thinking, "Is it possible that I did not explain the answer well?" However, since the Teacher spoke the concordant approval, "Excellent," Śāriputra was joyful that his own question was good; the noble Avalokiteśvara too was supremely joyful, knowing that his answer to the question turned out well; and the other retinues also gained delight and satisfaction, since they gained belief and their doubts were severed. Moreover, if some were to say here, "If this profound sūtra belongs to the sūtras of the middle turning, it is inappropriate for it to teach the Madhyamaka of other-emptiness," and, "If it teaches that, there would be no difference in profundity between the middle and final [turnings]," they should be answered as follows: The intention of all three turnings is also the Madhyamaka of other-emptiness, and even in the first and middle turnings there are some words that clearly teach it explicitly. In the turning that ascertains the ultimate, it is taught more clearly and extensively, without being hidden but made manifest or expounded boundlessly, than in both the [first] turning and the middle one. Thus, there is a difference of superior and inferior among the three turnings, and since their intention is also the same, those two faults do not apply. Therefore, regarding the explicit teaching of this sūtra, it clearly teaches the common other-emptiness, while it explains the uncommon meaning of the heart of the Sugata, which is permanent, steadfast, eternal, and possessing all aspects, by way of hidden meaning.
